newsitem.title: UK: UK minutes show BOE would prefer higher rates.
newsitem.headline: UK minutes show BOE would prefer higher rates.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George would prefer to see official interest rates at 6.0 percent rather than the present 5.75 percent, according to the minutes of his July 30 monetary meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
George said latest economic evidence showed a pickup in consumer-led demand.

"On that basis, the Bank saw no justificationn for further policy stimulus. In fact, as the Chancellor knew, the Bank would prefer short-term rates at 6.0 percent," the minutes summarised George as saying.
Still quoting George, the minutes contined:

"It was possible that this month's data exaggerated the underlying acceleration of demand. But the opposite risk was that if the acceleration continued through the summer and into the autumn, it would become increasingly difficult to moderate."
Clarke ruled that interest rates should remain unchanged "for the moment" because the latest economic data had tended to confirm expectations about the prospects for inflation.
"He was inclined to leave interest rates unchanged. If inflation pressures started to pick up as a result of stronger growth, there would clearly be a case for tightening policy."
"He was prepared to act pre-emptively, as he had done in 1994. But he saw no evidence yet of those pressures," the minutes said.

Clarke said he was extremely encouraged by the latest inflation and labour market data and noted almost universal agreement that the economy was now picking up despite "disappointing and surprising" preliminary figures showing just 0.4 percent growth in GDP in the second quarter.
"His expectation of stronger growth in the second half of the year was undiminished."
"In his view, this was to be welcomed but needed to be seen against the background of below-trend growth in recent quarters," the minutes said.

George agreed that recent data served to reinforce the prospect of weak inflationary pressures in the short run but said they also pointed to increasing strength of demand, especially consumption, in the period ahead.
In the discussion, the point was made that:
"While it might still be some time before the stronger survey evidence was reflected in official output data, there were increasing signs that activity had shifted up a gear."
"The downside risks to activity in the short term, identified at previous meetings, had receded again. This picture was consistent with the central expectation for inflation in official forecasts."
